# EEG theta power in Bangladeshi children: Associations with early experiences and cognitive outcomes

**Authors:** Eileen F. Sullivan; Ran Wei; Shahria Kakon; Talat Shama; Fahmida Tofail; William A. Petri; Rashidul Haque; Charles A. Nelson

**Affiliations:** aBoston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA, | bHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA, | cPeking University, Graduate School of Education, Beijing, China, | dInternational Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Dhaka, Bangladesh, | eUniversity of Virginia, Charlottesville, VA, USA, | fHarvard Graduate School of Education, Cambridge, MA, USA

## Abstract

Identifying the neural processes that underlie the association between children’s early adverse experiences and cognitive development could inform more effective intervention strategies. The goal of the current study (data collected 2015–2021) was to examine relations among early experiences at six months, electroencephalography (EEG) theta power at six months and two years, and cognitive outcomes at five years in Bangladeshi children (N = 115; 67 females). Results revealed that better nutritional status was associated with a slower increase in theta power from six months to two years and higher cognitive scores at five years. Higher frontocentral theta power at two years was related to better cognition at five years but did not mediate the association between nutritional status and cognition.

The first two years of life represent a period of heightened neural plasticity during which early experiences can have particularly strong influences on the brain and cognitive skills (Luby et al., 2020; Ellis et al., 2022). Understanding how early experiences become neurobiologically embedded and impact brain and cognitive development could inform the design of earlier and more targeted identification strategies and intervention programs for children.

In line with these goals, a large body of research examining the links between early experiences and neural correlates of cognition has emerged in recent decades. One area of particular focus has been on understanding how electroencephalography (EEG) power, or the strength of electrical signals generated from synchronous neural oscillations as measured by electrodes on the scalp, supports and indexes development (Anderson & Perone, 2018). Theta power, defined in the current study as slower oscillatory neural activity in the 4–6 Hz range, is one power band that has been repeatedly linked to both experiences and cognition early in life (Saby & Marshall, 2012; Begus & Bonawitz, 2020). Yet, compared to other power bands such as alpha, relatively less is known about the longitudinal development of theta power or how a range of early experiences more common in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are related to theta power (Saby & Marshall, 2012). Thus, in the current study we investigate how theta power in the first two years of life relates to early adverse experiences and later cognitive outcomes in children growing up in Bangladesh, a lower-middle income country.

An emerging literature base has begun to document how theta power develops over the first years of life. These studies vary in how EEG data are collected (e.g., resting state versus task-based) and how theta power is characterized (e.g., relative versus absolute), adding complexity to the interpretation of the existing evidence (Tan et al., 2024). The primary focus of this paper is on absolute theta power extracted from baseline (resting state) EEG data. (Relative power results are presented in the supplement for reference.) Longitudinal studies in the first two years of life have shown a rapid increase in absolute theta power during resting state paradigms early in infancy, followed by a slower increase or plateau from approximately nine to 24 months of age (Wilkinson et al., 2023; Gabard-Durnam et al., 2019). Relative theta power (the proportion of theta power compared to power in all frequency bands) has been shown to decrease over the first two years, part of a larger pattern of low frequency band power decreasing and higher frequency band power increasing over development (Marshall et al., 2004; Rico-Picó et al., 2023).

Resting state EEG studies have often found that lower absolute and relative theta power, particularly over frontal regions, are both linked to better performance on a range of cognitive and language assessments (Tan et al., 2024; Begus & Bonawitz, 2020). In infancy, higher relative theta power during rest was concurrently related to lower parent-reported ability of infants to orient and sustain attention at six to 12 months old (Perone & Gartstein, 2019). Lower absolute theta power during infancy has also been found to be longitudinally associated with higher language scores at two years in children with an elevated likelihood for autism spectrum disorder (Wilkinson et al., 2020). Additionally, evidence from the Bucharest Early Intervention Project (BEIP), a randomized control trial of foster care in Romania, revealed that lower relative and absolute theta power in two- to four-years-olds (some of whom were institutionalized) was associated with higher executive functioning skills at eight years old and intelligence quotients (IQ) at eighteen years old (Wade et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2023). Overall, higher resting state theta power is hypothesized to reflect a less mature developmental profile and is negatively associated with a range of cognitive outcomes from infancy through adolescence (Tan et al., 2024).

Resting state theta power has been found to be sensitive to a variety of distal (e.g., family income) and proximal early experiences (e.g., caregiving quality). Several studies have found links between family income and theta power. For instance, one study in young infants found that lower family income was related to lower absolute theta power at two months of age (Wilkinson et al., 2023). Yet, later in development an opposite pattern has been found, with lower family income associated with higher absolute theta power in four- to six-year-olds and eight- to fifteen-year-olds (Otero et al., 2003; Maguire & Schneider, 2019). Additional studies are needed to understand the development of these associations and generalizability of these findings. A variety of proximal experiences have also been found to be associated with resting state theta power, with most work focusing on relative power measures. Nutrition has been linked to theta power early in life. For example, one study in the United States found that infants who were breastfed show lower relative theta power in anterior regions than infants who were fed milk or soy formula at six months (Jing et al., 2010). The early caregiving environment has also been found to be associated with theta power. Findings from the BEIP study reveal that institutionalization, later placement in foster care, and lower caregiving quality were all related to higher relative theta power from two to four years old (Wade et al., 2024). Maternal stress, another key aspect of the caregiving environment, has been linked to higher relative theta power in infancy in studies in the United States (Troller-Renfree et al., 2020; Brandes-Aitken et al., 2023). Maternal stress was found to be associated with higher absolute theta power at 36 months but not six months in children in the same community in Dhaka as the current study participants (Jensen et al. 2021), aligning with other studies suggesting that associations between early experiences and EEG power may take time to emerge over development (Brito et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2019).

Overall, the existing literature provides a solid foundation on theta power and its links with early experiences and cognitive outcomes. Yet, important gaps in our understanding remain. For instance, additional longitudinal studies beginning in infancy are needed to uncover how early experiences may affect the developmental changes in theta power over infancy and childhood. Further work on absolute power is needed in infancy and early childhood, as absolute power has been found to have higher internal consistency during development (Lopez et al., 2023) and allows for direct examination of longitudinal changes in theta power without controlling for power in other frequency bands. Additional work from LMICs, or Majority World countries, will contribute to a better understanding of how cultural or contextual factors may influence theta power development. Theta power development could vary across cultures due to unique protective or adverse factors, differences in the relevance placed on certain skills, or the influence of cultural values and norms. Thus, to inform culturally relevant intervention strategies, it is essential to investigate the development of theta power within a specific culture instead of assuming evidence from high-income countries is universally generalizable.

Given the current gaps and promising future directions in the field, in the present study we investigated theta power in the first two years of life in children growing up in a low-income neighborhood in Dhaka, Bangladesh and examined how theta power may relate to several early experiences and later cognitive outcomes. While the primary focus of this study is on frontal theta power in light of strong links found with both early experiences and cognitive outcomes in previous research, theta power outside of frontal regions has also been related to early experiences (e.g., Sandre et al., 2024) and cognition (Tan et al., 2024). Thus, we present results with additional regions in the supplementary materials. This study was centered around three main aims. First, we sought to characterize absolute frontal theta power at six months and two years of age to better understand developmental differences in Bangladeshi children. We sought to confirm findings from previous studies and hypothesized that there would be an increase in theta power from six months to two years. Second, we examined whether measures of various early experiences at six months were associated with theta power at six months or the change in theta power between six months and two years. We hypothesized that higher levels of adverse circumstances would be linked to higher concurrent theta power and a faster increase in theta power between six months and two years. Third, we investigated whether early experiences at six months or theta power at two years were predictive of cognitive skills at five years of age. We hypothesized that higher socioeconomic status (SES), better nutrition, lower maternal stress, and lower absolute theta power would be related to better performance on both general and specific cognitive measures. The second and third aims were largely exploratory as we did not have a priori hypotheses about which early experience would be most strongly related to theta power and cognition. Lastly, we conducted an exploratory mediation analysis to examine whether theta power could explain any observed associations between early experiences and cognition. With these aims, we sought to understand how theta power may be a useful metric of the biological embedding of early experiences or as a predictor of later cognition.

## Methods

### Participants

Participants were Bangladeshi children living in the Mirpur district of Dhaka and were enrolled in the angladesh Early Adversity Neuroimaging (BEAN) study. The BEAN study is a longitudinal study of children’s brain and behavioral development, employing several neuroimaging and behavioral techniques. This paper is focused on one cohort of children enrolled at six months of age, with follow-up visits at two and five years of age. Data collection took place between 2015 and 2021. See Table 1 for exact ages and descriptive statistics of the sample. Families in the study had an average income of 511.93 Bangladeshi Takas (6.62 USD) per day at time of enrollment. Approximately 93% of families in the study sample were living in poverty (compared to 13.5% of families in Bangladesh overall), as defined as living on the current equivalent of $2.15 per person per day (National Institute of Population Research and Training & ICF, 2023). Mothers of study participants had received 4.81 years of formal education on average (SD = 3.87). Participants were recruited from a larger birth cohort study of Cryptosporidiosis in Bangladesh. Children were excluded from the study if they had a history of any neurological abnormalities, traumatic brain injuries, visual or auditory impairments, or were born less than 34 weeks gestational age. Measures of early experiences at six months, EEG data at six months and two years, and cognitive outcomes at five years were used in the current analyses. The original sample at six months of age was 130 children (74 females). The final dataset consisted of 115 children (67 females) with valid EEG data at six months (N = 89) and or two years (N = 86). The 15 families not included in the final dataset (due to dropout) had comparable demographics and adversity measures, except for a significantly lower adjusted family income compared to included families (Figure S1). Data were collected at a medical clinic in the Mirpur district by local psychologists and medical staff. This study was approved by the Ethics and Review Committee at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) and the Institutional Review Board at Boston Children’s Hospital.

### EEG Data Collection

Continuous EEG data were recorded using a 128-channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net (HGSN) with a NetAmps 300 input amplifier (Electrical Geodesic Inc., Eugene, OR). Each participant’s head circumference was measured and a net of appropriate size was selected. Participants sat on their parent’s lap on a chair approximately 65 cm from a screen in a dimly lit room. Resting state EEG data were collected for up to 120 seconds while children watched a screensaver with moving abstract shapes and calming sounds. Data were collected at a sampling rate of 500 Hz and impedances were limited to 100 kΩ.

### EEG Data Processing and Analysis Procedures

Data were pre-processed using the Harvard Automated Processing Pipeline for Electroencephalography (HAPPE) Version 4.0 (Gabard-Durnam et al., 2018) using Matlab R2020b. Channels of the HGSN net that were located around the outer rim and eyes were removed from analyses (Figure 1). Line noise was reduced at 50 Hz, as well as 25, 26, 27, and 28 Hz using the CleanLine EEGLAB plug-in (Mullen, 2012), as line noise was seen at these harmonic frequencies in prior analyses with the current dataset. Data were then filtered using EEGLAB’s Finite Impulse Response function with a 1 Hz high pass cutoff and 100 Hz low pass cutoff (Delorme & Makeig, 2004). Bad channels with high impedances, excessive movement, or artifacts were detected using the happe_detectBadChans function. Wavelet thresholding was then performed using the happe_wavThresh function, employing a soft empirical Bayesian level-dependent threshold, to correct for motion artifact (Lopez et al., 2022; Monachino et al., 2022). Independent component analysis (ICA) was used to remove remaining artifacts due to electromyographic (EMG) artifact using muscle ICLabel (MuscIL) (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019). Artifacts labeled as muscle artifact with more than a 25% probability were rejected and removed. Data were then segmented into two-second epochs. Segments were rejected if artifacts with a signal amplitude above 150 or below −150 microvolts remained. Data were then re-referenced to an average reference and converted to .set EEGLAB format.

The quality of the pre-processed data and pipeline performance was then checked using HAPPE Version 4.0’s built-in data and pipeline quality checks. At six months of age, 102 participants completed an EEG session. At two years of age, 94 participants completed an EEG session (with a loss of eight participants due to family not attending follow up visit, technical difficulties, or fussiness). Reasons for exclusion of EEG data within each timepoint can be found in Table 2. Participants’ data were removed from analyses if they had fewer than 80% of channels marked as acceptable out of 98 electrodes pre-processed (7% of 6-month-olds and 2.6% of two-year-olds excluded for this reason). Participants were rejected if their data had fewer than 20 segments remaining after segment rejection (0.9% of six-month-olds and two-year-olds excluded), as this is a typical threshold in similar analyses (e.g., Gabard-Durnam et al., 2019; Wilkinson et al., 2023). Participants were also removed if they had fewer than two acceptable channels in each region of interest (ROI). Primary regions of interest were Frontocentral, Frontal Left, and Frontal Right, each containing six channels (Figure 1). (Additional analyses with regions outside of frontal areas can be found in the supplement.) Participants were rejected if the r value of post pre waveleting was below 0.1 at five Hz (frequency of interest within theta band) (1.7% of six-month-olds and 0.9% of two-year-olds excluded). Participants were removed if data from one or more ROIs had a log theta power value > 3 SD below or above average the mean value within age (0.9% of six-month-olds and 0% of two-year-olds excluded).

While not used as rejection criteria, several other data and pipeline quality parameters were checked. The correlation (r value) between data before and after line noise reduction was evaluated at 50 Hz (M = .70 for six-month-olds; M = .83 for two-year-olds). No significant correlations between line noise reduction and theta power measurements were found for any ROI for six-month-olds (p-values > .222) or two-year-olds (p-values > .061). The percent of variance retained after wavelet thresholding (M = 52.16 for six-month-olds; M = 65.42 for two-year-olds) and the percentage of independent components rejected for each participant (M = 3.75 for six-month-olds; M = 1.91 for two-year-olds) were checked. The r value of pre to post waveleting for all frequencies was evaluated (M = .70 for six-month-olds; M = .78 for two-year-olds). Internal consistency values for each primary ROI and each timepoint are presented in Table S1.

After restricting the final dataset to participants with EEG data with adequate quality, 89 participants had valid data at six months old and 86 participants had valid data at two years old. Power spectral density (PSD) across frequencies and average absolute theta power, defined as power in the 4–6 Hz range based on prior literature with similar ages of participants (Wilkinson et al., 2020; Brandes-Aitken et al., 2023; Gabard-Durnam et al., 2019), were extracted for each ROI for each participant using a multitaper spectral analysis in the generatePower module in HAPPE Version 4.0 (using 4 slepian tapers, the default in the package). Absolute power measures were then log transformed (base 10). Absolute power was chosen because it has been shown to have higher internal consistency than relative power measures in developmental studies (Lopez et al., 2023), but relative power results are presented in the supplement to allow for comparison to existing studies.

### Measures of Early Adverse Experiences

#### Socioeconomic Status

Families’ SES was operationalized with years of formal maternal education and adjusted family daily income. Participants’ caregivers reported “total monthly family income” in Bangladeshi Takas (1 USD was equivalent to 77.27 Takas in 2016, when data was collected). Adjusted daily family income (in Takas) was then calculated by dividing daily family income by the number of individuals residing in the home. Maternal education levels, family income, and number of household members were orally self-reported by mothers at time of enrollment (when participants were six months) on a demographics questionnaire administered by local staff.

#### Nutritional Status

Children’s nutritional status was indexed with height-for-age Z-scores (HAZ). HAZ scores are Z-scores of the ratio of children’s height and age in reference to World Health Organization’s (WHO) growth standards using the WHO’s Anthro Plus software (Version 3.2.2). Children’s height and weight were measured at enrollment (six months of age) by staff in the Mirpur medical clinic. HAZ can be used to identify children who are stunted (HAZ < −2), a commonly used proxy measure for chronic malnourishment (e.g., Li et al., 2023).

#### Maternal stress

Maternal stress was measured using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) (Cohen et al., 1983). The PSS is a commonly used questionnaire designed to capture mothers’ thoughts and feelings during the last month. The measure consists of 10 items about how often mothers experienced a certain feeling, scored on a scale of zero = “never” to four = “very often”. Examples of questions include “In the last month, how often have you felt nervous and stressed?” and “In the last month, how often have you felt that things were going your way?”. Certain items were reverse coded so that higher scores reflected higher levels of perceived stress. The total PSS score was used for current analyses and was calculated by summing the scores on all ten items (maximum possible score of 40). The PSS was translated by two local bilingual psychologists separately and back translated. Each item of the original scale was then reviewed by an expert team of university teachers, clinicians, community leaders, and mothers. The scale was then pilot tested on 14 mothers by trained local psychologists before deployment in the current study. The PSS showed good test-retest reliability after a seven-day gap (r = .86). The measure showed adequate internal consistency, with a Cronbach’s alpha of .64 (Jensen et al.2021). PSS scores can be classified into three categories: low stress (scores of 0–13), moderate stress (scores of 14–26), and high stress (scores of 27–40). These categories have not been adapted to the local context, so were used only for descriptive purposes. Continuous PSS scores were used in analyses.

### Cognitive Outcomes

#### General Cognitive Development

The Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence – Third Edition (WPPSI-III) was administered by local psychologists when children were five years old to assess general cognitive development (Wechsler, 1991). The WPPSI is a behavioral assessment designed to assess both verbal and non-verbal reasoning skills in children. For the current analyses, the full-scale intelligence quotient (FSIQ) scores were used to capture general cognitive skills. Because the WPPSI was originally developed and normed for use in the United States, the WPPSI was culturally adapted to the context by local psychologists. Unfamiliar words and images were replaced with content more familiar to children growing up in Dhaka (e.g., Western oven replaced by local stove, hamburger replaced by banana, wagon replaced by rickshaw; see Table S2 for full details on adaptations). The translated version of the verbal comprehension scale was re-ranked to be in order of increasing difficulty after piloting 60 children. The WPPSI has been administered in Bangladesh in previous studies and found to have good test-retest reliability and significant relations with the Bayley developmental assessment in Bangladeshi children (Aboud, 2007; Hamadani et al., 2014).

#### Working Memory

The Paired Associates Learning (PAL) Task, as part of the Cambridge Neuropsychological Testing Automated Battery (CANTAB), was administered on an iPad at five years old to measure children’s working memory skills (Figure S2). The CANTAB is a tablet-based behavioral assessment instrument normed from ages four to 90 and has been used in over 100 countries, including Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan (Akter et al., 2015; Cambridge Cognition Limited, 2006). In the PAL task, children watched a screen with several gray boxes arranged in a circle. The number of boxes on the outside increased over time throughout the task to make it more challenging. In a random order, boxes were “opened” to briefly reveal what was underneath them one at a time. Under one or more boxes was a unique colorful geometric shape, while the rest of the boxes were empty. A geometric shape then appeared in the middle of the screen while the outer boxes were all closed. Children were asked to select which gray box contained the pattern that exactly matched the shape in the center. The variable of interest was the total number of errors (incorrect selections). In this way, lower number of errors (higher accuracy) were interpreted to represent better working memory performance on the task.

As the PAL working memory task was administered on an iPad through the CANTAB app, a questionnaire on families’ smart phone and tablet use was administered by local staff as an oral interview to caregivers. Performance on the PAL task was not significantly correlated with the average minutes children spent on screens per day (r = .087, p = .590), and thus time on screens was not used as a control variable in future analyses.

#### Inhibitory Control

Children’s inhibitory control skills were measured using a go no-go task at five years old (see Sullivan et al. 2022 for details on presentation of the task). Go no-go tasks are classic tests of cognitive control and inhibition. In this version of the task, children watched a screen while different animals flashed on the screen (Figure S2). Children were asked to press a response button if they saw a cat, dog, or cow on the screen (go trials – 70% of all trials) and to not press the response button if they saw a chicken on the screen (no-go trials – 30% of trials). Animals common in Bangladesh and familiar to local children were selected. The variable of interest was mean accuracy on the task (proportion of trials with correct responses). Accuracy on this task was also not correlated with time children spent on screens (r(34) = .297, p = .079).

### Analysis Plan

To characterize theta power in this sample (Aim One), power spectral density plots were created using RStudio Version 1.3.1093 and topographical maps of theta power were created using Matlab version R2020b. Linear mixed effects models were then run using the lme4 package in RStudio Version 1.3.1093 (Bates et al., 2015) to examine possible age or ROI differences in theta power. Model 1 included a random intercept for participant, allowing six-month theta power to vary across participants, and a random slope for timepoint, allowing the difference in theta power between six months and two years to vary across participants. The model also included fixed effects for timepoint (to investigate the amount of change in theta power between the six-month and two-year sessions) and ROI (Frontocentral, Frontal Left, and Frontal Right), as well as an interaction effect between timepoint and ROI to explore whether changes in theta power over time differed based on the region. Timepoint was used as a random slope and fixed effect instead of exact age of assessment given the focus of the study was developmental differences between six months and two years of age, the large gap between the visits gives us limited ability to make inferences about trajectories of change, and we had relatively low variability in age at each visit timepoint.

As an exploratory analysis, bivariate correlations between EEG, early experience, and cognitive measures were first calculated. Next, to examine whether early experiences were related to theta power (Aim Two), two additional linear mixed models were fit. Model 2 was fit to include all random and fixed effects as Model 1, as well as additional fixed effects for each early experience measure and the number of included EEG segments. Model 3 included all random and fixed effects as Model 2 and also fixed effects for interaction terms between timepoint and each of the early experience measures. One participant was missing income data and four participants were missing HAZ data, so mean imputation was used to impute this data to retain the same number of subjects across linear mixed models and allow for model comparison. Missing data were assumed to be missing completely at random (MCAR), and this assumption was upheld by Little’s MCAR test (X2 (177) = 196.82, p = .15). To evaluate model fit, Alkaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and log likelihoods were calculated. For the linear mixed models, each model was restricted to participants with valid EEG data. Likelihood ratio tests were used to compare model fit. Standard errors and 95% confidence intervals were computed to contextualize estimates (Wasserstein et al., 2019).

To examine whether early adverse experiences or theta power were related to cognitive outcomes (Aim Three), a series of multiple linear regressions were performed. The three cognitive outcomes for these regressions were general cognition (WPPSI FSIQ), working memory performance (total number of errors on the PAL task), and inhibition performance (mean accuracy on the go no-go task). Listwise deletion was used for all linear regressions, such that participants with missing data for any variable in the regression were excluded from that model. Sensitivity analyses were conducted with mean imputation of missing data for all variables used in linear regressions to retain the full sample of 115 and a similar pattern of results was found (Table S3). A power analysis was performed using G*Power version 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) for these models. To obtain a medium effect size (f2 = 0.15, α= 0.05) and a power (1 − β) of 0.80 with five predictors (maximum used in any model), 55 participants were needed. Sample sizes for these regressions ranged from 68 to 85 participants.

Lastly, a mediation analysis was performed using PROCESS version 43 in RStudio (Model 4: Simple mediation) (Hayes, 2022) with bootstrapping (5,000 resamples) to investigate whether theta power could partially explain relations between early experiences and cognitive outcomes. The model included child HAZ at six months as the predictor, FSIQ at five years as the outcome, and frontocentral theta power at two years as the potential mediator (chosen based on significant findings from the linear mixed models and linear regressions).

## Results

### Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics of participants’ age at each session, SES, early experience measures, and cognitive outcomes are displayed in Table 1. Approximately 16% of participants in this sample were stunted (HAZ < −2), slightly lower than the overall level of stunting of children under age five in Dhaka (21.5%). Mothers had an average score of 19 on the PSS (SD = 6.82). Thirteen percent of mothers reported high levels of perceived stress (scores ranging 27–40) and 68% of mothers reported moderate levels of perceived stress (scores ranging 14–26) (Cohen et al., 1983). Children’s average accuracy on the go no-go inhibition task was 82% (SD = 10%) to all trials. Children had 38.4 errors on average during the PAL task (SD = 18.29). The average FSIQ was 82.60 (SD = 11.51).

### Aim One: Characterizing Theta Power

To examine patterns of theta power development in this sample, we statistically tested whether theta power significantly differed across frontal regions of interest or ages, and whether the difference in theta power between six months and two years differed by ROI. To explore these questions, we built our first linear mixed model (Model 1) to include fixed effects for timepoint, ROI, and a timepoint × ROI interaction term, a random intercept for participant, and a random slope for timepoint (Table 3). Examining the random effects in the model, 36.4% of variance in Model 1 can be explained by the random intercept for individual participant, indicating substantial variation among participants’ baseline theta power at six months. Additionally, 56.3% of variance in Model 1 can be explained by the random slope for timepoint (six months or two years), indicating there is also substantial variation across participants in the amount of difference in theta power changes between the two EEG sessions.

The results from the fixed effects in Model 1 revealed higher theta power at two years old compared to six months old (B = 0.121, SE = 0.024, p < .001), suggesting a developmental increase in theta power during this time window. Figures 2 and 3 shows visualizations of PSD across frequencies and topographical plots of theta power, respectively, for the two age groups.

Examining differences among ROIs, we found that at six months old, participants had higher theta power in the Frontal Left (B = 0.078, SE = 0.010, p < .001) and Frontal Right (B = 0.077, SE = 0.010, p < .001) regions compared to the Frontocentral region (Figure 4). A post-hoc t-test revealed no significant difference between Frontal Left and Frontal Right at six months (t(177.88) = 0.047, p = .962), suggesting that theta power is not significantly lateralized at this age. To explore ROI differences at two years old, additional post-hoc t-tests were conducted. Two-year-olds had lower theta power in the Frontocentral ROI than the Frontal Left ROI (t(161.91) = −2.700, p = .008) (Figure 4). There were no significant differences in theta power between the Frontal Left and Frontal Right ROIs (t(169.49) = 1.021, p = .309) or between the Frontocentral and Frontal Right ROIs (t(165.17) = −1.735, p = .085) at two years old. The interactions between ROI and timepoint were not significant (p-values > .05), suggesting that the difference in between theta power at approximately six months and two years is comparable across the frontal and central regions. Overall, these results suggest that theta power is lower in the Frontocentral region than Frontal Left and Frontal Right at six months and two years, and the increase in theta power over this developmental window is similar across all ROIs tested.

### Aim Two: Examining Links Between Early Experiences and Theta Power

To assess whether early experiences were related to theta power, we fit two additional linear mixed models (Models 2 and 3; full results shown in Table S4). In Model 2, we investigate whether measures of early experience are related to baseline theta power at six months old by adding five additional fixed effects (income, maternal education, HAZ, maternal stress as early experience measures; sex as a control) to Model 1. A likelihood ratio test revealed that Model 2 (including early experience measures) did not have a significantly better fit than Model 1 (with no early experience measures) (χ2(5) = 9.357, p =.096). AIC and BIC estimates were also lower for Model 1 than for Model 2, providing further evidence that Model 1 is a better fit to our data. Overall, since early experience measures did not improve the model fit, we conclude that early experiences do not provide significantly more explanatory power to our model of theta power at six months. No early experience measures were significantly related to theta power, yet females had higher theta power than males (B = −0.061, SE = 0.028, p < .05).

We next investigated whether early experiences were related to the difference in theta power at six months and two years. To address this question, in Model 3, we built from Model 2 and added interaction effects between early experiences and timepoint as fixed effects to test whether the change in theta power between the two study sessions differed based on exposure level to various early experiences. Likelihood ratio tests revealed that Model 3 did not have better fit than Model 1 (χ2(10) =15.946, p = .101) or Model 2 (χ2(5) = 6.589, p = .253). Model 3 had higher AIC and BIC values than Models 1 and 2, indicating a worse fit. Thus, it appears that adding interactions between early experiences and timepoint did not add sufficient explanatory value of theta power. However, we did find a significant interaction between HAZ and timepoint (B = −0.057, SE = 0.026, p < .05), indicating that children who were better nourished had a slower increase in theta power from six months to two years. These models suggest that while exposure to early adverse experiences are not robust predictors of theta power early in life, nutrition may be related to how theta develops over the first two years of life. While not substantively interpreted here given sample size and power considerations, Models 1, 2, and 3 were also fit utilizing relative power for frontal regions (Table S5) for reference and comparison to other studies’ results. Model 3 was also run using absolute and relative power across additional regions outside of our primary ROIs (Table S6). Regions selected were frontal, occipital, central, temporal, and parietal, based off Sandre et al., 2024 (Figure S3).

### Aim Three: Examining Potential Predictors of Cognitive Outcomes

Having investigated patterns of theta power development and possible links to early experiences, we turned to our third aim: investigating whether early experiences or theta power are related to general cognition or specific executive functions. We first examined bivariate correlations between early experiences, theta power, and cognitive outcomes (Figure S4). We then performed a series of multiple linear regressions to investigate potential associations between measures of early experiences at six months and the three cognitive outcomes at five years: full-scale IQ (on the WPPSI), working memory (total errors on the PAL task), and inhibition (accuracy on the go no-go task) (Table 4). We found that HAZ was positively related to IQ (B = 4.657, SE = 1.388, p < .01), suggesting that children who are better nourished (as indexed by higher HAZ) tend to have higher IQ scores, even after controlling for family income, maternal education, and maternal stress. We also found that HAZ was negatively related to working memory errors (B = −7.321, SE = 2.406, p < .01), indicating that children who are better nourished have better working memory performance. Other than HAZ, no additional early experiences were significantly related to IQ or working memory errors. None of the early experience measures were significantly related to inhibition. These results indicate that many forms of early experience at six months do not appear to predict the cognitive outcomes measured in this study at five years. Yet, notably, nutrition in infancy is predictive of IQ and working memory in middle childhood, demonstrating how very early experiences may have lasting influences on certain aspects of cognition.

Next, we performed another series of multiple linear regressions to test whether absolute frontal theta power at two years old was associated with cognitive outcomes at five years (Table 4). (Results with relative frontal theta power, as well as absolute and relative theta power, are presented in Table S7). We found that theta power in the Frontocentral ROI at two years was positively related to IQ at five years (B = 26.138, SE = 12.257, p < .05), suggesting that children with higher theta power in this region at two years of age tend to have higher IQ scores at five years of age. Theta power in the Frontal Left and Frontal Right regions at two years were not related to IQ, and no theta power measures from our three ROIs were related to either working memory errors or inhibition (p-values > .05). At six months of age, theta power in the Frontocentral and Frontal Left ROIs were related to inhibition, but no associations were found between six-month theta power and IQ or working memory (Figure S4). While these results should be investigated further with a larger sample size, this pattern of findings may indicate that theta power at two years, especially in the frontocentral region, could potentially serve as an early predictor of general cognitive abilities, but is not a useful predictor of specific executive function skills.

As an exploratory analysis to investigate whether theta power at two years could explain associations between early experiences at six months and cognitive outcomes at five years, a mediation model was tested. We chose HAZ at six months as our independent variable and IQ at five years as our dependent variable because we found a significant association between these variables through multiple regression. We chose Frontocentral theta at two years to test as a mediator because it was found to be associated with IQ. The results of the mediation test revealed that the indirect effect of HAZ at six months on IQ at five years through Frontocentral theta power at two years was not significant (B = −0.047, bootstrapped SE = 0.360, bootstrapped 95% CI [−1.042, 0.477]). Thus, while we find an association between HAZ and IQ, as well as an association between Frontocentral theta power and IQ, these paths seem to operate somewhat independently as the path from HAZ to IQ does not appear to be explained by Frontocentral theta power.

## Discussion

In this study, we examined longitudinal relations among early adverse experiences, EEG theta power, and cognitive outcomes in children growing up in Dhaka, Bangladesh. We sought to understand whether theta power in the first two years of life could relate to early experiences or serve as a predictor of later cognitive outcomes in this context, with the eventual aim of informing culturally relevant interventions and identification strategies to support child development. We first examined the early socioeconomic, biological, and psychosocial experiences of children in our study. This study sample is drawn from a low-income urban neighborhood in the Mirpur area of the city of Dhaka, and is thus not representative of all of Bangladesh, which is comprised of both urban and rural areas with wide socioeconomic variability (Al-Maruf et al., 2022). There was a high prevalence of extreme poverty in the study sample, with higher levels of socioeconomic disadvantage compared to the rest of Bangladesh (National Institute of Population Research and Training & ICF, 2023). The majority of mothers (81%) reported moderate or high stress levels when their child was six months old, and 13% of children were chronically malnourished (as indexed by HAZ) at six months old. Importantly, even within this study sample, there was significant variation in SES, HAZ, and maternal stress.

### Developmental and Spatial Patterns of Theta Power

Theta power was next examined across age groups and regions of interest to characterize whether developmental patterns of this EEG feature are similar in this context to the existing literature generated mostly from high-income settings. Our finding that theta power was higher at two years old compared to at six months old aligns with our hypothesis, as well as with previous studies from high-income settings that have documented increases in theta power over infancy and early childhood (Gabard-Durnam et al., 2019; Wilkinson et al., 2023). Future longitudinal studies with denser sampling over the first two years of life are needed in Bangladesh and other LMICs to examine whether the developmental trajectory of theta power found in high-income settings (e.g., early sharp increase in infancy, then slower increase or plateau over the second year of life) (Gabard-Durnam et al., 2019; Wilkinson et al., 2023) is evident across populations, or whether context-specific growth curves are more appropriate. Our findings on the spatial distribution pattern of theta power in frontal areas of the brain indicate a largely similar spatial topography at six months and two years. These findings characterize theta power across regions of interest within the frontal lobe for the first time in this context, as much of the existing literature on theta power has focused on one ROI encompassing the frontal lobe. Further work on the distribution of theta within the frontal lobe is needed in other contexts to understand whether the developmental and spatial patterns found in this study are similar to findings in other populations.

### Relating Theta Power to Early Experiences

Relations between measures of early experiences and theta power were then tested to investigate whether features of children’s environment could help to explain the large amount of individual variation found in theta power. In contradiction to our hypothesis, early experiences were not related to theta power at six months or two years. These findings are not in line with much of the existing literature which has shown that maternal stress and income are related to higher theta power in infancy and later in development (Troller-Renfree et al., 2020; Brandes-Aitken et al., 2023; Maguire & Schneider, 2019; Otero et al., 2003). However, these results indings from a prior BEAN study analysis, which found that associations between early experiences and theta power were not seen at six months old (in the same cohort examined in the current analyses). Yet, in this prior analysis, associations were seen at three years old (in a separate cross-sectional cohort) (Jensen et al. 2021). Thus, it is plausible that we will start to see associations between early experiences and theta power emerge by three years of age (although the prior BEAN analysis used only one frontal ROI instead of three frontal ROIs in this paper, and thus these methodological differences could contribute to different results).

To delve into the timing and emergence of these relations, we next tested whether early experiences were related to the difference in theta power between approximately six months and two years. We found that children with higher HAZ (better nutritional status) have a smaller rate increase in theta power between six months and two years than children who have lower HAZ. Because the literature has shown that lower resting state theta power may reflect a more mature developmental profile, it is possible that better nutrition (higher HAZ) during infancy could be a protective factor and support neural development (as indexed by theta power). Yet, further work in Bangladesh and other LMIC populations is needed to understand what developmental trajectories should be considered expected or “optimal” in this setting before the current results can be properly contextualized and interpreted.

In summary, we find that better nutrition may be associated with a slower increase in theta power between six months and two years, but no early experience measures were related to theta power concurrently at six months or longitudinally at two years. One possible explanation for this pattern of findings is that early experiences may influence theta power developmental trajectories but not be as relevant to theta power at any one given timepoint. Alternatively, the impacts of early experiences may take time to emerge, as suggested by Jensen et al. (2021) and may not be evident by two years of age. We also may not be adequately capturing important context-specific and culturally relevant adverse or protective factors, or there may not be enough variation within this study sample to detect differences based on exposure to early experiences.

### Relating Early Experiences and Theta Power to Cognitive Outcomes

After examining links between early experiences and theta power, we tested whether early experiences were longitudinally related to cognitive outcomes at five years of age, as uncovering predictors of later cognition could help to identify children at risk of cognitive deficit or delays earlier when intervention is most effective. We found that children who were better nourished (as indexed by higher HAZ) in infancy tended to have higher IQ and better working memory performance (as indexed by lower number of errors) at five years. This finding is notable as it suggests that nutrition during infancy could have a lasting influence until at least five years of age, demonstrating the importance of children’s early nutritional environment, in line with previous literature establishing observational (e.g., Deoni et al., 2018) and causal (e.g., Ansuya et al., 2023) longitudinal relations between nutrition and cognition. We did not see associations between any other early experience measure and the cognitive outcomes, possibly because these measures of experience or cognition may not be well-suited to this population, were not adapted adequately to the cultural context, or there is more variation over childhood in these measures than nutritional status making it less likely to detect longitudinal associations over a five-year span.

Relations between theta power at two years and cognition at five years were then tested to assess whether theta power could serve as an early neural marker of a range of cognitive outcomes. We found that higher frontocentral theta power at two years was related to higher IQ at five years. This finding is in contradiction to our hypothesis based on prior findings that lower absolute resting state theta is linked to better performance on cognitive tests (Wade et al., 2020; Maguire & Schneider, 2019), yet much of this existing literature is based on studies looking at relative theta power (e.g., Tan et al., 2023), concurrent associations, children of different ages, or high-income settings. Therefore, future work should explore how these associations operate within and across various cultures and contexts. Of note, many task-based EEG studies have found that higher theta power or theta modulation during tasks that require attention and engagement is related to better performance on cognitive tests (showing an opposite pattern to resting-state theta power studies) (Tan et al., 2023). One possible explanation for our surprising finding of higher theta being related to higher IQ could be that the “resting state” EEG data that were collected while participants watched a moving screensaver could instead be operating more like a task-based paradigm in this context. Watching a screensaver may be more novel and interesting in the current study setting or require more attention due to distractions and loud noises from the surrounding urban neighborhood. Future studies should investigate how the stimuli, novelty, and context of resting state data collection affect theta power. We did not find any associations between theta power and performance on the working memory or inhibition task, which could indicate that theta power may be a better marker of general cognition rather than specific executive functions.

Notably, we did not find evidence that theta power was a significant mediator of the relation between HAZ at six months and IQ at five years. Thus, we conclude that the association between HAZ and IQ operates through pathways other than theta power at these timepoints, and alternative potential neural mechanisms should be explored (such as decomposed aperiodic and periodic components of power or functional connectivity measures).

### Limitations and Future Directions

While this study contributes to a deeper understanding of EEG theta power in an LMIC context, there are certain limitations and opportunities for future investigation to consider when interpreting findings. Firstly, while we sought to examine theta power at six months and two years to understand developmental differences, without denser sampling and additional timepoints we cannot comment on how theta power develops between these two timepoints. Furthermore, we chose to investigate absolute power as it has been shown to have higher internal consistency than relative power and could not fully consider both absolute and relative power due to power considerations given our sample size. Yet, it is important to acknowledge that differences in theta power between our two timepoints may be due to skull thicknesses or variation in the peak frequency of theta oscillations at these different ages. Also, we utilized the WPPSI as a cognitive outcome, and while this assessment was extensively adapted to the local context it is still possible that this test was biased. Thus, the replication of these results should be tested with a locally derived measure of cognition. Additionally, it is important to acknowledge that this study represents findings from a low-income, urban area in Bangladesh and are not generalizable to all of Bangladesh or all LMIC contexts. Furthermore, 15 families dropped out of the study following the enrollment visit (and drop-out status was related to family income), and thus the final sample may not be fully representative of the community. Lastly, although we utilize a longitudinal study design to establish temporal precedence among variables, we cannot draw causal conclusions from these findings as they are drawn from observational data.

In the future, we hope to extend the current analyses in several ways. We plan to examine additional parameters of theta power, including characterizing periodic and aperiodic components (Tan et al., 2024; Wilkinson et al., 2024) and conducting time frequency analyses of EEG data collected during the go no-go inhibition task (Sullivan et al. 2022). While we focused on theta power in the current paper because of links found with experiences and cognition in the prior literature and a need to understand the longitudinal development of this frequency band, in the future we plan to investigate whether a similar pattern of results is seen for other frequency bands. We also plan to expand our sample by including data from additional higher-income cohorts of children recently collected as part of the BEAN study to widen the generalizability of the study. A follow-up study of the current study sample at eight and eleven years of age is in progress, which will allow us to study relations with cognition and academic performance in older children. Additionally, a nutrition intervention is underway in the same neighborhood in Dhaka, affording the opportunity to draw from casual data to examine whether theta power development is influenced by nutritional supplementation early in life.

### Conclusion

With this study of theta power in infants and young children in Bangladesh, we have further demonstrated the feasibility and utility of conducting large-scale longitudinal neuroimaging studies in LMICs. We have shown that nutrition during infancy could play a particularly important role in cognitive development, but the impacts of nutrition on cognitive outcomes may not be immediately evident and instead emerge more slowly across the childhood period. Our observation that higher theta power was related to better general cognition, in contrast to studies in high-income settings finding the opposite association with both absolute and relative, warrants further investigation into how cultural and contextual factors may play a role in explaining variation in how theta power supports or indexes cognition. These findings underscore the need for additional longitudinal studies in LMICs that investigate the emergence and timing of associations among experiences, neural development, and cognitive outcomes.
