# Early adversity alters brain architecture and increases susceptibility to mental health disorders

**Authors:** Charles A. Nelson; Eileen F. Sullivan; Viviane Valdes

**Affiliations:** 1Laboratories of Cognitive Neuroscience, Division of Developmental Medicine, Department of Paediatrics, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA. | 2Department of Paediatrics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. | 3Harvard Graduate School of Education, Cambridge, MA, USA.

## Abstract

Each year, millions of children around the world are exposed to a host of adverse experiences early in life. These include various forms of maltreatment, growing up in unsafe neighbourhoods, and witnessing intimate partner violence. These experiences exact a toll on the brain development and mental health of children. In this Review, we attempt to explain how brain architecture and circuitry are affected by exposure to such early adversity, which in turn increases susceptibility to mental health disorders later in life. We begin defining what we mean by early adversity and then summarize the experience-dependent nature of postnatal brain development. Within this context, we discuss times in development when the brain is particularly receptive to experience (critical periods) and, thus, is more vulnerable to adverse experiences. Drawing from studies with both rodent and non-human primate models and neuroimaging research with humans, we next discuss how the circuitry of the brain is affected by early-life adversity, with a focus on the subsequent effects upon neural network development. We then review the mental health consequences of adverse experiences in early life across mental health disorders and within specific dimensions of psychopathology. We conclude by offering a conceptual model of the pathway that links exposure to adversity early in life to these mental health outcomes later in life, and we provide suggestions for future research.

## Introduction

Millions of children each year experience various types of adversity early in life that increase their likelihood of developing a mental health disorder. To meet diagnostic criteria, the symptoms of an individual must lead to marked distress or impairment in daily functioning, affecting their emotional, psychological and/or behavioural well-being. Berens et al.1 conceptualized early adversity as negative childhood experiences associated with increased lifetime risk of poorer psychological, physical and social health outcomes. Children can experience a myriad of different types of adversity early in life, including both psychosocial (maltreatment, such as abuse or neglect, and household-level adversities, such as intimate partner violence or parental mental illness) and biological (malnutrition, water and/or air pollution, and other hazards, such as toxin exposure)2–4 forms of exposure (Fig. 1a). These early adverse experiences function as deviations from expected environmental inputs that can disrupt typical developmental trajectories, have deleterious effects on the development of children, and result in negative health outcomes, including psychopathology.

From a broad public health perspective, the statistics on exposure to early adversity are sobering. Globally, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has estimated that one-half of the world’s children under 18 years of age experience physical or harsh punishment or abuse in any given year5, and the United Nations estimates that between 133 and 275 million children globally witness violence between primary caregivers6. Moreover, between March 2020 and May 2022, more than 10 million children were orphaned because of COVID-19 (refs. 7,8). In the US, between 2011 and 2021, over 330,000 children lost a parent to drug overdose9. Last, more than half of individuals in the US experience at least one type of childhood adversity and one-fifth experience three or more types (physical, emotional or sexual abuse, physical or emotional neglect, household substance use, mental health disorders, parental separation or divorce, incarceration, or domestic violence), with the highest risks of exposure to early-life adversity occuring among multiracial, Latino and Black Americans10.

Although there is a well-established link between exposure to early adversity and later mental health outcomes11–19, less is known about what mediates this link; specifically, how do these experiences shift the course of brain development and subsequently increase the likelihood that a child will develop a mental health disorder? The overarching goal of this Review is to draw from both the animal and human neuroscience literatures on early adversity to elucidate how brain development is altered by exposure to adversity during critical periods of brain development, which in turn elevates the risk of developing psychopathology later in life. A secondary goal is to consider how an understanding of the links between early adversity, brain development and developmental psychopathology might inform the design, deployment and optimal timing of more efficacious interventions.

We begin by discussing how adverse exposures can influence brain development and how this association can be affected by a multitude of factors, including developmental timing and the various forms and features of adverse experiences. Next, we discuss what we have learned from the rodent, non-human and human primate literatures on adversity-driven changes in brain development. To complement this work, we then examine the neural correlates associated with the development of psychopathology, with a focus on studies that examine neural network development (primarily functional connectivity) and associations with mental health disorders (across disorders and within specific dimensions of disorders). We do not discuss other biological mechanisms that may mediate links between early adversity and mental health outcomes, including the extensive literature linking early-life stress, the development of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, and mental health outcomes20–22. We also do not discuss recent and exciting work on how early-life stress may alter immune function, which in turn may increase susceptibility to mental health disorders23,24. We conclude by offering a conceptual model that attempts to link the potential pathways through which adverse exposures early in life could lead to changes in certain neural networks that increase susceptibility to psychopathology later in life, and then we provide suggestions for future research and policy implications.

### Developmental consequences of early adversity

It is well-established that postnatal experiences that occur during sensitive or critical periods of development have a profound impact on brain development25. Sensitive periods represent times in development when the brain is particularly receptive to experiences in the form of patterned activity (such as repetitions in the speech train). As sensitive periods close, greater and greater effort is required to modify neural circuits26. By contrast, critical periods represent times in development during which experience must occur for development to proceed along a typical developmental trajectory; once a critical period has closed, neural circuits become exceptionally difficult if not impossible to reopen26–28. The opening and closing of critical periods is regulated by excitatory–inhibitory balance, which is primarily mediated by glutamatergic and GABAergic neurotransmitters29–32. For example, visual and auditory input is needed to support the development of normal visual and auditory function; similarly, adequate caregiving and language input, again during a sensitive period (generally the first 2 years of life), is required for healthy attachment relationships and for language to develop26,33,34 (Fig. 2). In the context of human development, sensitive periods probably underpin most aspects of behavioural development, whereas critical periods are more applicable to rodents and other non-primate mammals and to sensory and sensorimotor system development. In addition, no single sensitive period exists, but rather sensitive periods cascade and differ by domain35–37 (Fig. 2; compare visual versus language development).

Building on prior work by Greenough et al.28, Nelson and Gabard-Durnam25 and McLaughlin et al.38, we conceptualize early-life adversity as a deviation from the expectable environment. Our general argument is that although human genomes provide a foundational blueprint for brain development, experience then refines neural architecture (through experience-dependent plasticity during sensitive periods). It is further assumed that all members of any species expect certain elements of the environment to be present at birth to facilitate healthy brain development; for example, a human infant will have access to patterned light, auditory and linguistic input, and caregiving. Greenough et al.28 referred to this as experience-expectant development. When a deviation from this environment occurs — such as inadequate caregiving or a lack of visual or auditory input — development is perturbed. A myriad of factors can disrupt brain development, including the particular type of psychosocial or biological adverse experience (Fig. 1a). The developmental sequelae of any of these adverse exposures can be influenced by multiple environmental features. For instance, adverse experiences can occur in different contexts, including at the individual (prematurity, infectious diseases), family (domestic violence, household crowding), community (poor sanitation, neighbourhood violence) or societal level (lack of economic opportunity, discrimination) (Fig. 1b). A child’s individual experience of adverse exposures could also be influenced by severity (level of disruption to expectable environment), timing (developmental window of exposure) and chronicity (frequency and duration) (Fig. 1c). Although not the focus of this Review, the genetic background or socioeconomic and cultural environment of an individual may also modify the impact of early-life adversity on them (Fig. 1d).

Behavioural development often reflects gene × environment interactions39–41, which in turn can manifest in a range of individual differences: for example, the child who is exposed to an enriched, positive environment yet develops mental health issues later in life, or the child who is exposed to an impoverished, profoundly negative environment yet thrives later in life. However, at a population level, exposure to adversity during these sensitive periods, in most cases, biases trajectories of brain development in a negative direction, leading to a host of developmental sequelae, including mental health disorders. It is worth noting that a recent meta-analysis of observational studies has failed to observe a specific period in development when maltreatment exerts a particularly strong effect on mental health outcomes42. However, this meta-analytic work has noted that the studies included were largely underpowered and relied on retrospective methods, which may have been limited in detecting salient timing effects. In the sections that follow, we discuss how alterations in brain architecture and circuitry may mediate adverse mental health outcomes following exposure to early adversity.

### Putative neural correlates underpinning the effects of early adversity

In this section, we provide an overarching high-level synthesis of key evidence from both animal and human studies on adversity-driven changes in brain development, which could serve as a potential link between exposure to early adversity and the development of mental health challenges later in life. Animal and human studies both have relative advantages and disadvantages in modelling exposure to early adversity (Box 1). For example, one can directly manipulate environments and circuits in animal studies while also visualizing the brain at the level of individual neurons and their elements (dendrites, axons); however, the vast differences among the behavioural repertoires and brain architectures of species (for example, the proportion of the cortex dedicated to the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is vastly smaller in rodents than in humans) limit their usefulness in modelling human psychopathology. Conversely, studies of humans offer findings that could be more readily translated but are largely limited to non-invasive neuroimaging techniques. These non-invasive techniques generate insights at the level of larger brain structures and circuits rather than individual neurons but offer insight into the relations between brain structures, circuits and behaviour. As a result, both animal and human evidence are integral to answering distinct but complementary questions about the neurobiological consequences of adversity.

### Evidence from work with rodents

Studies with rodents are well-positioned to offer causal, mechanistic insight into the molecular-level, cellular-level and circuit-level impacts of early adversity on neurodevelopment43,44. A few common paradigms have been deployed in rodents to model certain forms of adversity (such as deprivation or abuse)45. Paradigms designed to shed light on the effects of material deprivation, such as limited bedding and nesting manipulations, have been used as a model of early-life stress (perhaps a proxy for poverty in humans). Material deprivation has been shown to lead to reduced amygdala grey matter volume (GMV) and decreased proliferation and/or neurogenesis, as well as altered connections between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and basolateral amygdala, in both rats and mice45–47. Physical pain paradigms, thought to model aspects of physical abuse in humans, have been shown to cause alterations in the network of brain areas involved in fear processing (linking the basolateral amygdala, ventral tegmentum and mPFC), the expression of genes involved in neurogenesis, and dendrite morphology in the amygdala in rats48,49. Maternal separation in rats and mice, or paradigms involving removal of pups from being reared by their biological mother for some period of time (perhaps a proxy for emotional neglect in humans), is linked to higher activity (neuronal firing as indexed by FOS expression) in the hypothalamus and limbic regions, but the amount of increase depends on the timing and duration of maternal separation (with most lasting effects seen when separation occurs before postnatal day 15)45,50. Importantly, there is a wide variation (in both chronicity and timing) of material deprivation, physical pain and maternal separation protocols51. Although not discussed, additional early-life stress models such as sibling separation, nutritional deprivation, male intruder and low maternal care have also been deployed in rodents to explore the consequences of a wide array of adverse exposures51.

As in humans, adverse experiences for rodents in early life do not always occur in isolation and instead can co-occur and interact. Thus, it is important to examine the brain changes related to the interplay of different types of early-life adversity. One study by Barr et al.52 has demonstrated how the effects of physical pain are moderated by the social context of the pain, providing an example of the interrelations of different types of early-life experience. In that study, infant rat pups exposed to a tail shock in the presence of their mother showed lower levels of behavioural reactivity and expression differences in genes implicated in neural development compared with those exposed to the shock without her present, underscoring the role of a buffering relationship in protecting against adverse outcomes. Notably, the effects of shock that occurs early in life when the mother is or is not present have a differential impact on adult behaviours depending on the timing of exposure (fewer differences seen if shocks occurred on postnatal day 9 compared with postnatal day 12), further demonstrating the role of sensitive periods in regulating the response of the brain to adversity exposure. The interactive effects of different forms of early adversity have also been shown in studies revealing that experience of material deprivation paradigms tends to provoke lower-quality caregiving when rodents become mothers53, which could exacerbate the neural consequences of material deprivation alone for their offspring54.

Together, the rodent literature offers key causal evidence on the neural consequences of various types of disruption to the expectable rearing environment and indicates the importance of examining interactive effects of adverse experiences. However, direct translation of these findings to humans can be limited, given the vast differences between the rodent and human brains.

### Evidence from work with non-human primates

The study of non-human primates may bring us a step closer to shedding light on the human condition, given their greater similarities in the duration of lifespan, developmental trajectories and basic brain architecture. A long history of examining the consequences of early-life adversity on behavioural development of non-human primates exists55,56, such as the classic studies by Harlow and, later, Suomi57–59, examining maternal separation and social isolation.

In a study examining whether the age at which infant monkeys are separated from their mothers has a differential impact on development. Animals separated at 1 week appeared withdrawn, became anxious when approached by another monkey, and exhibited various behavioural stereotypies when confronted by another animal. By contrast, animals separated from their mothers at 1 month were anxious except in the presence of another monkey, exhibiting atypical behaviours that mirrored the behavioural presentations of an attachment disorder in humans. After monitoring the behaviour of prematurely separated monkeys for several weeks, the authors then cross-fostered them with new mothers. The 3-month separated animals exhibited typical behaviour. By contrast, the 1-week separated animals seemed unable to form a connection with the foster mother and became more distressed and aggressive in their presence, whereas the 1-month separated animals appeared to form a relationship with their new mother and to display some remediation of their previous atypical behaviours (such as beginning to play with other monkeys). Similar effects have also been observed in infant rhesus monkeys cross-fostered to mothers either with a history of maltreating their infants or with no such history. Here, the infant monkeys cross-fostered with the former experienced more behavioural sequelae and alterations in hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis activity than those cross-fostered with the latter60.

Few non-human primate studies have focused on the neural correlates associated with exposure to maternal separation. In one study, rhesus monkeys that experienced maternal separation early in life showed decreased white matter density in the brain compared to maternally reared monkeys61. In the separation and cross-fostering study described above60, mRNA was extracted from the right medial temporal lobe, primarily the amygdala, of a subset of the monkeys at several years of age62. In these adult monkeys, GUCY1A3 (which encodes a subunit of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) that catalyses the conversion of GTP to the second messenger cGMP) showed differential expression between the 1-week prematurely separated and maternally reared groups and the 1-week and 1-month prematurely separated groups. Moreover, GUCY1A3 expression positively correlated with acute social-comforting behaviour and longer-term close social behaviour, whereas it negatively correlated with self-comforting behaviours. This pattern of findings is consistent with the behavioural phenotype observed among the 1-week versus 1-month separated animals. An extensive body of work has also focused on rhesus macaques that maltreat their infants (see ref. 63 for an example). Macaques that experienced maltreatment showed increased functional connectivity (communication and synchronization of neural activity among brain regions), in this case measured between the amygdala and several regions, including the PFC64.

Collectively, the work from both rodents (reviewed in ref. 45) and non-human primates (reviewed in ref. 65) suggests that structures within the limbic system (particularly the amygdala) and PFC are altered after exposure to various types of psychosocial forms of early adversity, including family separation, physical abuse and emotional neglect. Importantly, the connections between these regions can often be those most influenced by adverse experiences in humans (Fig. 3a), a point we elaborate on below.

### Evidence from work with humans

We now turn to the human neuroimaging literature for more direct insight into when early-life adversity occurs and how it relates to the developing human brain (acknowledging that ex vivo imaging comes with limited ability to infer causality and that most studies with humans are observational and, thus, correlational; Box 1). Associations between adversity and neurodevelopment have been well-documented reviewed in refs. 25,66,67 and 68). We briefly synthesize this existing evidence, focusing on types of adversity, such as neglect and abuse (Fig. 1a), that have been modelled in the animal literature.

Poverty (which we consider a complex, distal form of early-life adversity that can be accompanied by more proximal adversities such as material or resource deprivation, elevated levels of stress, and housing, food or safety insecurity) is associated with several changes in human brain connectivity. For example, weaker structural connectivity (anatomical connections such as white matter tracts) between brain regions, as assessed with structural MRI, has been observed in the PFC, hippocampus and amygdala. Moreover, reduced functional connectivity measured with resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) has also been observed across multiple brain regions (including, but not limited to, the default mode network (DMN), which comprises several key brain regions, including the mPFC, posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, inferior parietal lobule, and parts of the medial temporal lobe and is involved in various domains of cognitive and social processing)69,70. Poverty is also linked to changes in the tempo of brain development, such that postnatal experiences are associated with delays in brain development71, whereas prenatal exposure is associated with accelerated brain development (see ref. 72 for an in-depth discussion of the effects of poverty on the tempo of brain development). Because children growing up in poverty are nearly always exposed to poverty prenatally, these findings may simply reflect the amount of or duration of adversity exposure across both time periods.

Turning now to the specific effects of neglect on brain development, drawing from data collected in the Adolescent Brain and Child Development (ABCD) study, Beck et al.73 sought to examine the association between different types of adversity and brain development. They reported that adolescents who experienced early-life emotional neglect showed evidence of younger-looking (less mature) brains, whereas those who experienced caregiver psychopathology, trauma or family aggression showed evidence of older-looking (more mature) brains. Across two separate long-term studies of previously institutionalized children (the English–Romanian Adoptees Study74,75 and the Bucharest Early Intervention Project (BEIP)76–78, in which all of the children experienced psychosocial deprivation early in life), children with a history of institutional care showed reduced total brain volumes compared to never-institutionalized children, and they also showed dramatic reductions in both GMVs and white matter volumes (WMVs). Studies of previously institutionalized children adopted into homes in the USA have also reported changes in specific brain structures, including the amygdala, hippocampus and corpus collosum72,79.

Institutional care in early life has been also related to a more adultlike pattern of increased connectivity between the mPFC and amygdala as indexed by resting-state fMRI (whereas never-institutionalized children show decreased functional connectivity between these regions)74. In the BEIP, a randomized control trial of foster care as an alternative to institutional care, children randomly assigned to remain in institutional care showed lower integrity of the uncinate fasciculus (a white matter tract connecting the medial temporal lobe and the PFC) and less cortical thinning in the PFC (a normative process thought to reflect synaptic pruning) than children who were placed in foster care75. In addition, children randomly assigned to foster care placement before 2 years of age showed greater cortical thinning than those placed after 2 years of age, indicative of a sensitive period. Moreover, across the first two decades of life, children randomly assigned to continued institutional care consistently showed reduced electroencephalography (EEG) power across multiple scalp regions compared to never-institutionalized children; importantly, children randomly assigned to foster care showed improvement in their EEG profiles if placement occurred before approximately 2 years of age, providing further evidence of a sensitive period76–78.

Child abuse (experiences of physical, psychological and/or sexual abuse that excludes neglect) has been associated with a host of changes in brain structure, including in the ventromedial PFC, amygdala and corpus collosum80–82. Such maltreatment is also related to differences in structural connectivity (including in the corpus collosum and superior longitudinal fasciculus) and resting-state functional connectivity (including heightened connectivity among the amygdala, the DMN and prefrontal regulatory networks)83,84. It has also been linked to decreased resting-state functional connectivity within the salience network (SN), which is implicated in a broad range of functions (such as executive control and in maintaining vigilance and arousal) and is composed of the anterior insula, the anterior cingulate cortex, and subcortical structures including the amygdala and thalamus51. Threat-based early-life adverse exposures more broadly have also been linked to increased activation in the striatum and decreased fronto-striatal connectivity82. Importantly, adverse experiences in early life often co-occur, as many children may be exposed to more than one psychosocial or biological stressor and/or hazard in their environment. In this vein, exposure to multiple types of early-life adversity has been associated with reduced and increased within-network functional connectivity in frontoparietal networks and the DMN, respectively85.

Overall, early-life adversity in humans has been associated with structural and functional alterations in multiple brain systems, yet the directionality and strength of these relations appear to depend on the particular brain network and the type and timing of the adverse exposure85,86. Given the high co-occurrence of low socioeconomic status and other types of more proximal adversity such as neglect or abuse, future research with larger sample sizes and intervention designs are needed to disentangle the effects of distinct forms of adversity from those related to low socioeconomic status.

### Evidence across species

One seemingly intractable dilemma in comparing the human neuroimaging literature to work with rodents and non-human primates is that it is only in animal models that we can directly visualize circuits and cells, whereas in the human, we must suffice with proxies for metabolic (such as functional near infrared spectroscopy) or physiologic (such as EEG) activity. In addition, although MRI facilitates the drawing of reasonable inferences about structural connections (owing to advances in tractography and diffusion imaging), it is important to note that functional connectivity findings derived from fMRI and EEG are correlational in nature, as they reveal which brain areas are activated at the same time.

Despite these challenges in comparing rodents to both human and non-human primates (particularly in prefrontal areas, given the dramatic differences in size and cytoarchitecture of the PFC in rodents versus primates), several general conclusions can be drawn across species (Fig. 3b). First, adversity-related differences are seen in similar brain regions across species, including the amygdala and PFC. Furthermore, earlier and repeated or longer adverse experiences have been repeatedly associated with more marked alterations in the brain, which can be explained by heightened malleability of the brain during sensitive periods early in development67. In addition, different types of adversity appear to have somewhat differential effects on the brain in both animals and humans, the topic to which we turn our attention next54.

### Neural correlates of developmental psychopathology

In an early effort to explain why different types of adversity appear to have differential effects on brain and behavioural development, McLaughlin and Sheridan proposed a dimensional model of adversity87. They posited that deprivation-based and threat-based adversities affect the brain through different neural pathways, with deprivation (neglect, limited resources) often operating through changes to frontoparietal regions, and threat (emotional abuse, maltreatment) often operating through changes to the hippocampus, amygdala and mPFC82. Moreover, exposure to deprivation and threat in early life appears to have differential effects on cognition, emotion processing and mental health88. This model has recently expanded to include a third dimension, that of unpredictability89,90. Less predictable environments are associated with prolonged amygdala activation90 and altered development of white matter tracts implicated in memory (uncinate fasciculus and cingulum) in humans91. Unpredictability has also been found to be related to cognitive deficits in rodents, non-human primates and humans91.

However, it is worth noting that this dimensional view has not fully resolved the issue of accounting for multiple other aspects of the experience of adversity of an individual, which continue to plague the field92. First, most children exposed to adversity typically experience multiple forms simultaneously68. Second, the developmental brain age of a child (a child born prematurely versus full term) clearly has an impact on whether, and when, adversity will influence the course of development. Last, how to model multiple features of adversity beyond this two-dimensional view — including other features such as type, severity, frequency, duration, chronicity and timing (both onset and offset; Fig. 1) — has proven to be a thorny issue both statistically and biologically93. These issues all require further attention.

In the preceding sections, we, like other authors, have emphasized the effects of early adversity on specific brain circuits, which in turn map onto specific forms of psychopathology (such as anxiety versus depression). In the following section, we turn our discussion to how adversity maps onto changes in brain development that are common across many (as opposed to specific) disorders.

### Neural correlates common across disorders

Some research has documented differences in structural and functional connectivity that are common across mental health disorders. It should be noted that much of this work has focused on older children and adolescents, and a relative minority of the existing work has been able to integrate clear longitudinal links ranging from the experience of adversity to changes in the brain and subsequently to behavioural differences that confer risk for psychopathology (especially with adequately powered samples).

In terms of GMV, global GMV loss has been observed across a majority of brain regions in relation to general psychopathology symptoms in the 9–11-year-old American children enrolled in the ABCD study94. In analyses that controlled for total GMV, associations between general psychopathology and GMV loss were particularly evident in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral accumbens area and left-hemispheric amygdala, with greater GMV observed in right-hemispheric cerebellum94. Similarly, in a large cohort study in the Netherlands (Generation R), decreased global WMV was also associated with higher levels of general psychopathology in 6–10-year-old children95.

With regard to connectivity, one study that linked experiences of adversity (across 32 types of biological or psychosocial exposure) to psychopathology (across 10 mental health disorders) used longitudinal data from the ABCD study and found that differences in structural connectivity were most evident within the DMN and the SN96. Throughout adolescence and across all disorders, differential maturation of myelinated white matter tracts that connect the PFC to temporo-limbic areas has been noted97,98. These maturational changes may be functionally relevant, as reduced functional segregation between networks has been documented as an important marker of psychopathology across multiple disorders, especially between the SN, DMN and frontoparietal network (FPN; composed of the dorsolateral PFC, the posterior parietal cortex, and other related areas such as the anterior cingulate cortex and associated with a broad range of functions including executive control, working memory, attention regulation and goal-directed decision-making)97,99–101.

Existing meta-analytic research (193 studies, 15,892 participants and 6 diverse mental health disorders) in adults (21 to 60 years of age) has found GMV loss in the dorsal anterior cingulate and right-hemispheric and left-hemispheric insula across these disorders102. Independent analyses at later time points have found that lower GMV in these regions is associated with poorer subsequent executive functioning102. Further research is needed to elucidate whether these grey matter changes account for subsequent differences in functional connectivity observed within and between other networks and/or whether shared biological processes may account for both102. Importantly, the extent of neural network dysconnectivity observed in the brain is closely linked with symptom severity in individuals with mental health disorders. For instance, the extent of slowed maturation of myelinated white matter tracts linking the frontal cortex to temporo-limbic regions during adolescence has been related to a higher symptom load, such that greater disruptions in microstructural connectivity are associated with increased symptoms of psychopathology97,98.

### Neural correlates within specific disorder domains

Although a broader literature has documented differences in connectivity across mental health disorders, many of these differences do not always align neatly with existing categorical diagnostic conceptualizations. Some work has started to leverage findings from neuroimaging (among youth 8 to 22 years of age) to delineate differences at the circuit level that can inform brain-based dimensions of psychopathology100 (Fig. 4).

For instance, recent neuroimaging evidence from late childhood through young adulthood suggests that mood dimensions (suicidality, depression, mania) appear to be characterized by increases in functional connectivity between the ventral attention network (superior parietal lobule, intraparietal sulcus, superior colliculus) and the SN (anterior insula, anterior cingulate cortex)100. Increased connectivity between these networks could bias the attentional system towards specific types of stimulus, resulting in different disorders or symptoms (for example, bias towards negative stimuli and low mood with depression, feelings of hopelessness with suicidality, and exaggerated responses to positive stimuli with mania)103. Moreover, individuals with psychosis had the greatest functional connectivity between the SN and FPN100. This increased SN–FPN functional connectivity may reflect differences observed in psychosis whereby individuals exhibit difficulty in adaptively engaging with or controlling behaviour in the context of shifting goals and salience of external stimuli or self-referential thinking. For instance, heightened attribution of significance to specific stimuli can form the basis for positive symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions104,105.

The types of psychopathology associated with fear, such as social phobia and agoraphobia, can be distinguished by within-network connectivity of the FPN100. Stronger within-network functional connectivity in the FPN may reflect overactive top–down systems attempting to regulate fear responses and intrusive thoughts in individuals with those disorders106. Research examining externalizing behaviour dimensions prominently demonstrated that changes exist in functional connectivity between the FPN and other networks, including lower connectivity with the DMN and greater connectivity with the frontoparietal control network95,100. Lowered FPN–DMN connectivity could explain reduced levels of introspection and self-monitoring that may result in increased impulsivity and lapses in attention106. Increased connectivity with the frontoparietal control network may also explain the increased goal-directed behaviours observed in individuals with externalizing disorders (even at the expense of breaking social norms or in the face of consequences), as well as compensatory processes to manage reduced neural network efficiency107,108.

### Neurodevelopmental processes and onset of psychopathology

The emergence of psychopathology, especially the presentation of specific neurodevelopmental differences or the onset of disorders during different stages of development, could be related to the timing of neurodevelopmental processes. Sensitive periods, during which there may be heightened plasticity in major neural systems and related developmental domains, may provide a broad timeline for conceptually understanding how disruptions at particular time points may manifest behaviourally at that time, or have cascading behavioural manifestations at subsequent developmental stages (Fig. 2). We now begin to synthesize some of the existing evidence on neurodevelopmental changes that occur from early childhood through adolescence in conjunction with the discussed evidence of neural correlates in the context of psychopathology. However, we would like to underscore that more research is needed to systematically link how the timing of each normative or aberrant change in brain networks affects aspects of related developmental domains (such as socioemotional development) and specific behavioural symptom manifestations.

A substantial proportion of dendritic growth and synaptogenesis occurs through infancy and the beginning of childhood109. Synaptic pruning processes also occur during childhood to eventually form the basis for organized brain networks in late childhood109. Children with psychopathology (6–11 years of age) demonstrate reduced global GMV, especially in the hippocampus, accumbens and amygdala, alongside reductions in global WMV94,95. Connections within specific networks are probably most prominently refined during childhood109, perhaps explaining why structural and functional dysconnectivity within the DMN and/or SN (two networks that prominently develop during childhood) is most strongly associated with psychopathology in children96. Early experiences coupled with genetic and neurobiological changes (such as neuromodulation or regional volumetric differences) tend to contribute to the exact connectivity patterns within and ultimately between networks. For example, heightened functional connectivity in the DMN could contribute to excessive focus on internal thoughts (feared stimuli for people with phobias, separation from caregiver for people with separation anxiety, intrusive thoughts for people with obsessive compulsive disorder), whereas in the SN, it could produce heightened responses (exaggerated emotional responses for feared stimuli in people with anxiety disorders)110.

Adolescence is marked by the maturation of the FPN, in addition to improved connectivity between the FPN and other networks (such as the SN and DMN)111. Myelination and synaptic pruning processes during adolescence allow this network to become more specialized and efficient111. Consequently, improvements are typically seen throughout adolescence in executive functioning, regulation of emotional responses, cognitive flexibility and metacognitive thinking (self-referential thought processes about one’s cognitive processing)112. At the same time, hormonal changes during this period (such as production of testosterone and oestrogen) can also contribute to heightened emotional reactivity and increased focus on short-term rewards and/or novelty seeking, as the limbic system and striatum are particularly sensitive to these changes113. The lack of integration between sensitized limbic and striatal responses, coupled with an underdeveloped FPN, can create a period of vulnerability for psychopathology during adolescence113.

Throughout late childhood and adolescence, differential communication between the PFC and temporo-limbic regions may contribute to observed effects on executive functions (inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility), producing the observed differences in cognitive control of attention and emotion regulation (emotional processing, memory and heightened emotional and/or stress responses) that characterize psychopathology across disorders114. Reduced functional segregation between networks (such as the DMN and FPN) may also facilitate excessive rumination (internally oriented and self-referential thoughts) that are also commonly seen in the context of psychopathology (such as in people with anxiety and mood disorders)114.

Together, the evidence reviewed suggests that certain dimensions such as deprivation, threat and unpredictability may influence neurodevelopment through partially distinct pathways, although modelling these effects has proven challenging owing to the frequent co-occurrence of adversities and variability in experiences of adversity. Studies have also identified some shared and disorder-specific neural correlates for psychopathology, although most research has been cross-sectional with limited integration of longitudinal evidence that can systematically link adversity to brain changes and subsequent psychopathology.

### A neurobiological framework for understanding early adversity and psychopathology

On the basis of our review of these findings, we propose a conceptual framework that may explain the potential pathways through which adverse exposures could lead to changes in certain neural networks, creating downstream consequences for the risk of developing psychopathology (Fig. 5). In this framework, various features of adversity exposure (type, context, chronicity and severity) influence a person’s internal experience of his or her environment. Adversity in early life in turn results in changes to brain areas including the hippocampus, amygdala, PFC and frontoparietal regions more broadly82. The SN, DMN, FPN and other networks prominently featured in the discussed findings on the neural basis of the development of psychopathology often encompass these regions97,99–101. The differential connectivity within these networks could be associated with subsequent alterations to between-network connectivity patterns (through either shared underlying processes such as grey matter changes and/or within-network changes that impact between-network connectivity). Thus, early-life adversity-driven brain changes could heighten risk for the development of psychopathology.

Importantly, these pathways are not deterministic, and a wide array of individual differences in outcomes exist (with many individuals demonstrating resilience in the face of adversity in early life). Individual differences probably also arise from the moderating influences of genetics, epigenetics and distal environmental factors such as the sociocultural context (Fig. 1d). Furthermore, the effects of early adversity can differ according to the developmental timing of exposures because of the wide variation in times when certain neural circuits are most sensitive to the input of experience (Fig. 2). An emerging body of research has also begun to examine differences in brain structure that are associated with resilience and increased functioning. A recent systematic review by Eaton et al.115 found that resilience was associated with increased GMV in frontal regions, tighter coupling between the PFC and amygdala, larger ventral striatum volume and increased anatomical connectivity in the corpus callosum. Two reviews also report that individuals with experiences of adversity who have better mental health outcomes tend to have decreased resting-state functional connectivity between the amygdala and SN and the amygdala and the DMN115,116. Last, two reviews also find evidence for increased GMV and WMV in the hippocampus in individuals who show resilience experiencing adversity in early life115,116.

Although this body of research has made great strides in delineating structural and functional brain changes associated with resilience for psychopathology in the context of early-life adversity, important questions remain. What might explain individual differences? Are the differences observed in brain structure the result of pre-existing differences, or are there brain changes that occur following experiences of adversity? Answering these questions will require researchers to assess brain development as a longitudinal process before and after experiences of adversity to monitor pre-existing differences in structure and neuroplastic changes that may occur as a result of exposure to adversity in early life that contribute to resilient processes or outcomes115. Last, this foreshadows perhaps the most important question: how can we harness research findings to promote resilience among vulnerable, at-risk children?115.

### Suggestions for future research directions

Despite its potential for generating the strongest inferential evidence in humans, one topic that has received relatively scant attention in the literature is the need for more intervention studies. For example, most intervention studies target behaviour (such as reduction in symptoms), but will it be possible in the future to target neural networks? Moreover, most extant clinical trials continue to use behavioural outcomes as a test of efficacy, but why not incorporate imaging modalities to shed light on underlying brain activity? Increasing our awareness of the inferential ability of various imaging modalities and prioritizing those with the potential for drawing causal inferences will be important to more precisely capture the pathways from early adversity to psychopathology (see Box 1 for a visual depiction of inferential ability across research modalities).

Research designs that build bridges across multiple methodological approaches, species and disciplines will be best suited to provide the evidence grade needed to answer the most poignant questions remaining. For example, research approaches integrating interventions with a randomized control arm(s), neuroimaging modalities and longitudinal designs may be particularly powerful tools to enhance inferential ability in humans. As a randomized controlled trial focusing on foster care as an alternative to institutional care, the BEIP provides a powerful exemplar. Now in its 25th year, it has clearly demonstrated not only the hazards children raised in institutional care may face but also the benefits of placing such children, at an early age, into high-quality foster care. Furthermore, these benefits have been reported across multiple scales in the BEIP, including cellular, structural, electrophysiological, behavioural and psychological75,77,78,117–125.

Translational research that can bridge species, such as basic science studies with animals and those studying humans, the former of which is required to shed light on causal mechanisms and the latter of which facilitates external generalizability to the human condition, may also enhance our understanding of the pathways that connect early-life adversity with increased susceptibility to psychopathology. Research that can span multiple disciplines, such as studies integrating gene × environment interactions or modelling epigenetic changes that mediate adversity exposures in early life and subsequent outcomes, may shed light on the role of individual differences (in both response to exposure and in response to treatment). Across the board, prioritizing large sample sizes to capture variability and repeated measures to shed light on dynamic temporal changes will be invaluable.

Finally, and most imperatively, we must build bridges and translate evidence beyond our research spheres. If our ultimate goal is to improve the lives of children exposed to early adversity, we must link arms with those in a position to legislate and implement programmes and policies that can fundamentally influence the health of societies. Here, we are reminded of a well-known quote from Nelson Mandela, that “there can be no keener revelation of a society’s soul than the way in which it treats its children”126.

## Conclusions

Well-established links exist between exposure to adversity early in life and the development of psychopathology later in life, coupled with changes in a variety of neural systems. The nature, timing and duration of the adversity exposure interact with the genetic makeup of an individual to influence developmental outcomes (Fig. 1). The context for these gene × environment interactions is also important to consider. (Is there a buffering relationship in the life of a child? Is a child growing up in a low-resource setting where they may be exposed to multiple forms of adversity?).

Several topics require further examination. First, in the context of early-life adversity, an important consideration is how to weigh various features of experience, such as the nature of the adversity (harsh physical punishment versus verbal abuse), the timing of its onset (infancy versus early childhood) and its duration (time-limited versus persistent across all of childhood). Finding effective ways to integrate multiple features of experience, or to effectively isolate features of experience, to model the effects of adversity in early life on developmental trajectories will be crucial. Second, exposure to adversity is not deterministic as much as probabilistic; thus, examining how individual differences in outcomes may constrain developmental trajectories and outcomes will be necessary. Last, in this Review, we have focused most on the consequences of adversity that occurs early in life, but many forms of adversity can extend throughout the life course, and we must examine how mutually exclusive experiences of adversity early or later in life, or continuous experiences of adversity, may differentially impact outcomes.

In addition, several authors127,128 have recently argued that a focus on the deficits that result from exposure to early-life adversity fails to capture adaptations children will make in response to adversity that may manifest as ‘hidden talents’. It is certainly true that children exposed to adversity in early life adapt to their environments and, in so doing, may develop skills that aid them in coping in such environments, for example, being exceptionally good at reading faces (undoubtedly an adaptation when being raised in an abusive household; see ref. 129 for an example) or reaching out to strangers for comfort (a common trait among profoundly neglected children, who have had to cope with not having had their psychological needs met; see ref. 130 for an example). Moreover, it is also true that not all children exposed to adversity will develop psychopathology later in life; protective factors can operate at the individual level to prevent children from developing behavioural or psychological sequelae131. However, adaptations to an atypical environment (such as an abusive home) may prove maladaptive in typical environments (for example, a psychologically deprived 2-year-old child who walks off with a complete stranger). Furthermore, more research is needed to determine the extent to which fostering supportive environments and strengths of adversity-exposed children actually promotes more positive mental health outcomes.

In the context of psychopathology, the field currently operates largely within a categorical conceptualization. However, for an individual, psychopathology exists on a continuum and evolves throughout the life course, a reality that must be considered in future research. Furthermore, cascading effects of psychopathology symptoms that manifest very early in life (such as anxiety) must be accounted for, as these can greatly influence whether the individual will experience persistent and more severe symptoms later in life (particularly among those who do not receive treatment or other adequate buffering early in life).

In closing, we began this Review by defining early adversity and then discussed its impacts on brain development. Synthesizing across the rodent, non-human primate and human literatures, we showed that structures in the medial temporal lobe (the amygdala and hippocampus in particular) and the PFC are all affected by early-life adversity and mediate associations with altered neural network development, which in turn is associated with psychopathology later in development. It would be misleading to think that early in life is the only time in development at which adversity heightens the risk of developing problems in mental health; however, it is certainly the case that in these early years, the brain is at its most vulnerable. Given that early childhood may be a period of heightened neuroplasticity and vulnerability, interventions that are able to capitalize on this window through prevention strategies are particularly important. As circuit-specific processes for the development of psychopathology are further elucidated, developmentally timed and individualized interventions may be possible to target specific underlying neural substrates that ultimately produce risk for psychopathology throughout the lifespan.

As data analysis pipelines grow more complex in brain imaging research, understanding how methodological choices affect results is essential for ensuring reproducibility and transparency. This is especially relevant for functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS), a rapidly growing technique for assessing brain function in naturalistic settings and across the lifespan, yet one that still lacks standardized analysis approaches. In the fNIRS Reproducibility Study Hub (FRESH) initiative, we asked 38 research teams worldwide to independently analyze the same two fNIRS datasets. Despite using different pipelines, nearly 80% of teams agreed on group-level results, particularly when hypotheses were strongly supported by literature. Teams with higher self-reported analysis conﬁdence, which correlated with years of fNIRS experience, showed greater agreement. At the individual level, agreement was lower but improved with better data quality. The main sources of variability wererelated to how poor-quality data were handled, howresponseswere modeled, and how statistical analyses were conducted. These ﬁndings suggest that while ﬂexible analytical tools are valuable, clearer methodological and reporting standards could greatly enhance reproducibility. By identifying key drivers of variability, this study highlights current challenges and offers direction for improving transparency and reliability in fNIRS research.

Failures to replicate or reproduce published work have raised major concerns across several ﬁelds in science1–3. These reports have catalyzed both meta-research to explore the factors leading to diminished replication and reproduction rates4–8, and the launch of initiatives focused on improving these critical aspects of scientiﬁc research9–11. In particular, the ﬁeld of functional neuroimaging has progressively intensiﬁed its efforts to address the challenges of replicability and reproducibility12,13. A signiﬁcant part of the problem in neuroimaging relates to the complexity of the analysis. As neuroimaging data analysis has grown increasingly complex over recent decades14,15, it has become essential to ensure transparency in reporting analysis details to support reproducibility12,16–19. Current analysis pipelines encompass multiple stages, including data selection criteria, preprocessing options, selection of data elements (e.g., regions of interest), subsequent post-processing options, and an array of statistical models for hypothesis testing, with a multitude of parameters for each of these stages14. This diversity in processing and analysis options provides considerable ﬂexibility in analyzing the same dataset in various ways15,16,19, thereby enabling the exploration of a broader spectrum of research questions and accommodating different assumptions.

While analytical ﬂexibility represents a signiﬁcant advancement in the evolution of quantitative science, especially in handling high-dimensional data, it also poses challenges. Varying analysis pipelines can produce markedly divergent results, potentially leading to altered interpretations or even contradictory outcomes15,20,21. Analytical ﬂexibility also leads to analytical variability: when researchers can select from a broad spectrum of possible and justiﬁable analytical options, they are likely to make different choices. This freedom diminishes the comparability of results between studies, and even within the same study22–27. Moreover, due to the extensive arrayofpreprocessingand analysisoptions,researchersmightbeinclined to initially test pipelines aligning most with their expectations and exclusively report these outcomes. This approach, inﬂuenced by expectation and selection bias, results in undisclosed manipulation of analytical ﬂexibility, ultimately undermining its reliability and credibility13. Experiments conducted in collaboration with research communities have been instrumental in assessing the impact of analytical variability. In these studies, researchers are given the same dataset and test pre-speciﬁed hypotheses using analytical methods that they consider most suitable. Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (fNIRS) is another neuroimaging tool that has seen signiﬁcant growth over the past decades. This optical imaging method utilizes near-infrared light to measure changes in brain hemoglobin concentrations33–35. The portability, ease of use, accessibility, and relatively low cost of fNIRS, compared to fMRI, highlight its substantial potential for routine use in scientiﬁc, clinical, and commercial settings. It is particularly advantageous in populations or experimental paradigms where fMRI is less suitable, for instance, in low-to-middle income countries, or for neurodevelopmental research on infants and children. This adaptability allows for more complex paradigms with high ecological validity and low restrictions on natural movements and behaviors, but can also introduce additional variability into data analysis. The quality of fNIRS signals can be inﬂuenced by hair and skin characteristics36, requiring tailored preprocessing and analysis approaches, which further adds to the variability across analysis pipelines. Moreover, the ongoing development of new hardware and analytical pipelines contributes to this variability. Despite sharing similarities with EEG and fMRI, fNIRS has unique features and has been used in experimental designs that necessitate careful consideration regarding analytical ﬂexibility. Directly applying conclusions from other techniques to fNIRS is not straightforward. As the adoption of fNIRS expands across various ﬁelds, research at the community level is needed to assess a) how analytical variability manifests across the spectrum of analyticalchoices and b) how these different choices affectanalysis results and conclusions that can be drawn from identical fNIRS data. Initial investigations suggest considerable analytical variability across fNIRS pipelinesettings37–39.However,adetailedanalysisfocusingonthisvariability within fNIRS has yet to be conducted. Building upon previous investigations, the fNIRS Reproducibility Study Hub (FRESH) project explored the wide-ranging analysis methods employed within the fNIRS research community. By extending previous efforts, we quantiﬁed the variability in results when different researchers assessed the same dataset both at the group and individual levels. Given the complexity of experimental protocols and data analysis pipelines and the lack of standardization in fNIRS research40,41, understanding these variations is essential for progress. More importantly, addressing such variability in a period of increasing fNIRS signiﬁcance in neuroscience is a crucial step toward establishing standards in the ﬁeld. For this purpose, this study invited members of the global fNIRS community to participate in a multi-lab analysis experiment. Researchers were provided with two fNIRS datasets, a brief description of the experimental protocols, and a list of pre-deﬁned group-level and individual-level hypotheses related to research questions that could be investigated with these datasets. Researchers were assigned the task of testing these hypotheses. Importantly, researchers were not provided with instructions on how to perform these tasks other than based on their own expertise and best judgment. Details of the experimental protocol and fNIRS acquisition are provided in the Methods section. The ﬁrst dataset (Dataset I) comprised fNIRS recordings obtained from an auditory paradigm, which included speech, auditory noise stimuli, and silence, each lasting ~5 s. The hypotheses tested using this dataset were focused on group-level analyses: H1. Speech stimuli evoke responses in the left Heschl’s gyri (HG); H2. Speech stimuli evoke larger responses in the left HG than the noise stimuli; H3. Speech stimuli evoke larger responses in the left HG than the right HG; H4. Speech stimuli evoke response in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG); H5. Speech stimuli evoke larger responses in the LIFG than noise; H6. Speech stimuli evoke responses in the occipital cortex; H7. The silence condition evokes a response in the occipital cortex.

Among these, H142,43 and H2 are strongly supported by existing literature44,45, while H7 is strongly negated. Hypotheses H3-H6 are expected to be true but have less robust support from prior studies46–49. The second dataset (Dataset II) was derived from a motor experiment in which participants performed repeated right- and left-hand ﬁnger tapping for 2 and 3 s. The hypotheses for this dataset focused on individuallevel analysis: H1. Left-hand ﬁnger tapping (FT) of 2 s duration evokes a response in the contralateral primary motor cortex; H2. Left- and right-hand FT of 2 s duration, conditions combined, evokes a response in the contralateral primary motor cortex; H3. Left- and right-hand FT of 2 and 3 s duration, conditions combined, evokes a response in the contralateral primary motor cortex; H4. Left- and right-hand FT of 3 s duration, conditions combined, evokes a greater response in the contralateral primary motor cortex than left- and right-hand FT of 2-s duration, conditions combined. The ﬁrst three hypotheses are strongly supported by existing literature, while support for H4 is less conclusive50–53. After completing data analysis, researchers were asked to submit their results using a speciﬁcally designed form that inquired about the statistical outcomes for all pre-speciﬁed hypotheses. In a follow-up questionnaire, researchers were requested to provide further details about their analysis pipeline, including speciﬁcs about preprocessing and analysis steps theyhad performed. In this work, we synthesize and interpret the diversity of analysis approaches within the fNIRS community. Brieﬂy, we observed substantial variability in analysis pipelines, with no two teams using the same approach. Despite this, we found high agreement on group-level results, especially for hypotheses strongly supported by prior research. Agreement is lower for individual-level analyses but improves with better data quality. The main sources of variability across teams are linked to pruning choices, hemodynamic response function models, and the analysis space used for statistical inference. These ﬁndings reveal the extent and nature of analytical variability and its potential implications for research outcomes based on fNIRS.

Discussion Noninvasive neuroimaging techniques have revolutionized our understanding of the human brain, opening up new avenues in various scientiﬁc ﬁelds. As technology has advanced, facilitating more ﬂexible experimental protocols, it has also increased variability in data analysis, affecting the consistency of conclusions drawn from neuroimaging techniques, as seen with fMRI and EEG. Our results show that fNIRS faces similar challenges. Over the past decade, fNIRS has become a reliable and widely adopted tool35, particularly in experiments where other techniques fall short, due to its ﬂexibility and lower operational threshold compared to fMRI. However, while it is easy to acquire interpretable signals, assessing their meaningfulness remains difﬁ- cult. In addition, rapid technological advances have outpaced the standardization of data analysis, making it crucial to understand how different analysis pipelines impact scientiﬁc consistency. The results presented in this work shed light on this issue and provide insights for other neuroimaging techniques by exploring the inﬂuence of analysis ﬂexibility and other key factors that contribute to variability in outcomes, such as researcher conﬁdence. Overall, we observed substantial variability across teams in hypothesis testing, particularly at the individual level. It is important to note that, because the data originated from different sources, any direct comparison between group- and individual-level agreement is prone to bias from confounding factors such as variations in data quality. Despite this limitation, higher agreement rates (>80%) were seen in most group-level hypotheses (5 out of 7 hypotheses), indicating more consistent outcomes when individual variations are treated as noise or measurement error. Notably, the high percentage of agreement among teams for hypotheses with strong literature support reinforces the potential of fNIRS as a reliable neuroimaging technique, especially in the context of group-level analysis grounded in well-supported research contexts. As the strength of evidence for a hypothesis correlates with the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), these results imply that higher expected CNRs tend to result in greater agreement among teams, regardless of differences in the analysis pipelines used for fNIRS group-level studies. In contrast, individual-level hypotheses showed lower overall agreement, with only two hypotheses achieving levels of agreement comparable to those observed at the group level, and in only two out of 10 participants. This discrepancy likely arises from the greater sensitivity of individual-level analyses to intrinsic differences in anatomy and physiology, which makes individual outcomes more dependent on speciﬁc choices in the analysis

pipeline (e.g., exclusion criteria resulting in the removal of different trials and/or fNIRS channels across subjects). Despite the lower agreement observed in individual-level analyses compared to group-level analyses, the degree of agreement among groups consistently mirrored the strength of literature support for each hypothesis, with weak hypotheses resulting in lower agreement. Importantly, individual-level analyses revealed a clear effect of data quality (assessed by SNR) on the consistency of hypothesis testing outcomes: participants with higher SNR yielded greater agreement in their results. While this aligns with the expectation that higher-quality data produce more reliable outcomes, it is important to acknowledge that many factors inﬂuence SNR in fNIRS, including those related to population diversity and speciﬁc physiological or anatomical characteristics. These challenges are particularly relevant when collecting data from globally representative populations, where achieving high SNR can be more difﬁcult. In our study, the limited number of participants in Dataset II constrained our ability to statistically examine the relationship between participant demographics, SNR, and outcome agreements. Nonetheless, the observed impact of data quality on reproducibility does not diminish the importance of advancing equity and inclusion in neuroimaging research, and further highlights the need to develop more robust data analysis methods and increase sample size. No two teams adopted identical workﬂows, echoing ﬁndings from a previous study on variability in fMRI25. The ﬂexibility in choosing analysis pipelines led to considerable differences in the methods used, particularly in signal preprocessing and statistical testing. Recent efforts to establish best practices aim to enhance reproducibility, particularly for these stages40. For instance, the impact of confounding systemic signals on fNIRS is wellrecognized,alongwiththeimportanceofmethodologicallyaddressingthese by including additional systemic information in the analysis whenever possible, such as short-channel measurements as proxies for systemic physiology, which can greatly reduce false discovery rates56,57. Many groups (79%) used GLM for regression of systemic signals, while only a few (20%) used less robust methods like block averaging, which does not account for systemic physiological effects. Among GLM users, a slight majority (46% versus 33%) opted for AR- IRLS over OLS, as it effectively reduces false positives by accounting for the intrinsic temporal correlation of fNIRS signals through autoregressive models with optimal order selection58. Choices for the HRF regressor varied across six variants, from those allowing extensive shape ﬁtting like the FIR model,tothose with minimal parameterssuch as the Canonicalmodel. This variety highlights the need to establish a consensus on selecting HRF regressors. Regarding the additional regressors to the HRF, 70% of the groups that employed GLM used short-channel-based information. It is also worth noting that the majority of groups applied temporal smoothing (90%) to the fNIRS signal, using band-pass (70%) or low-pass (20%) ﬁltering. Therefore, these ﬁlter weights need to be accommodated in the estimation of temporal correlation with GLM40,58. Ignoring these correlations can lead to biased estimates of degrees of freedom and standard error, thereby invalidating statistical tests. A slight majority (52%) used HbO for statistical testing, as it generally shows a stronger response than HbR, though it is more susceptible to taskrelated systemic physiological changes39, potentially leading to a higher false discovery rate. Groups also varied in their approach to deﬁning the signal space for statistical testing, with 53% using Regions of Interest (ROIs) to reduce spontaneous noise and improve reliability, while 29% conducted their analyses at the channel level, which can increase sensitivity to spatial variability, especially in studies with low-density fNIRS setups lacking detailed spatial information. Pre-experiment optode registration can reduce this issue by ensuring consistent placement of optodes, thus enhancing reproducibility59. When anatomical registration is properly performed, translating data from the channel space to either the ROI or voxel spaces generally results in less variability60,61. A small amount (15%) utilized a combination of both ROI and channel-based methods. Second, the datasets used in this study were chosen based on their availability and adherence to current best practices in fNIRS acquisition. Both datasets were collected in healthy, young adults using commercial continuous-wave fNIRS devices from the same manufacturer. While this choice helped control for some sources of variability,itlimitsthegeneralizabilityofourﬁndingstodatasetscollectedin other populations (e.g., infants, elderly) or acquired with other devices or fNIRS modalities, such as time-domain (TD) or frequency-domain (FD) fNIRS. Regarding the experimental paradigm, we selected the ﬁnger-tapping task for its standard use in fNIRS, ensuring familiarity among researchers and offering little novelty from a neuroscience perspective. Overall, these design choices were intended to minimize other sources of variability unrelated to analysis pipelines, as more complex paradigms might have introduced additional variability or limited the number of researchers able to participate. This focus on simplicity, while suitable for our goals, limits the exploration of more advanced approaches, such as the ones employing multimodal analysis and artiﬁcial intelligence. These emerging methods represent exciting avenues for fNIRS research in the coming years and may even help standardize pipelines. Lastly, the formulation of the hypotheses might have inﬂuenced analytical choices. Although we aimed to provide clear, objective hypotheses for testing and offered an open forum for clariﬁcations, varying interpretations across groups could lead to differences in testing and reporting. Taken together, our ﬁndings suggest substantial levels of analytical variability in fNIRS, moderated by researchers’ experience and conﬁdence. Researchers use the degrees of freedom available in analyzing complex, high-dimensional fNIRS datasets, some of which were identiﬁed only after speciﬁcally querying them in a follow-up questionnaire. These results highlight the need for greater transparency and support for the adoption of open-science practices to enhance reproducibility and replicability in fNIRS research19,40,41. These efforts can reduce variability and enhance reproducibility, particularly in typical functional neuroimaging protocols1,69. However, it is important to recognize that consistency and reproducibility in outcomes do not equate to accuracy, as consistent results do not automatically reﬂect “ground truth”. Moving forward, future efforts should shift from describing variability to assessing the accuracy of data analysis pipelinesandevaluatinghowdifferentprocessingstepsinﬂuencehowcloselythe results align with expected outcomes. Hypothesis Outcomes Reporting We collected data from groups through two separate questionnaires: an Initial Survey and a Follow-up Questionnaire. The Initial Survey required groups to indicate for each hypothesis 1) whether it was conﬁrmed (“yes”), refuted (“no”), or “not investigated”, 2) the outcome of any statistical tests (e.g., p-value, credible interval, or conﬁdence intervals), if they were conducted, and 3) additional notes, along with a description of their analysis. The hypotheses given to the groups for the auditory and motor datasets are detailed in the Introduction section. Speciﬁcally for the motor dataset, groups had to submit individual reports for each of the ten participants. The Follow-up Questionnaire was sent to all groups approximately six weeks after the Initial Survey’s deadline, requesting that theyprovide further detailson the (1) programminglanguage and/oranalysis toolboxesused,(2) various steps of their analysis pipeline (from preprocessing to statistical analysis), and (3) their self-reported conﬁdence both in their analysis skills and in the results submitted. For each analysis step mentioned in the questionnaire, groups could specify whether they employed the default settings of the analysis toolbox or, if not, the parameters used in their analysis.

Analysis of Hypothesis Outcomes The data collected from the questionnaires were analyzed by an independent group of researchers who had not submitted any reports themselves. This meta-analysis included a description of the demographics of the researchers, an examination of the responses to hypothesis testing and their association with the self-reported conﬁdence levels, and an exploration of the different stages of the analysis pipelines and their effect on hypothesis testing outcomes. All analyses were carried out either in MATLAB (2023a, MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) or in Python.

The relationship between the analysis steps (independent variables) and the hypothesis testing outcomes (dependent variable) across teams was investigated using binary logistic regression. The outcomeofhypothesistestingwasindicatedbyabinaryvariable,asreported by each team. As each independent variable includes multiple subcategories (e.g., ﬁltering can be divided into four categories - band-pass, high-pass, low-pass, and no ﬁltering), we selected the most-commonly chosen category by the teams as the reference category. The logistic regression model was performed with the ‘ﬁtglm’ function in MATLAB. Giventhe binarynatureof the dependentvariable, the binomial distribution was selected to appropriately model the response. The logistic link function, speciﬁcally the logit link, was applied to establish the connection between the linear predictor and the probability of observing a signiﬁcant hypothesis testing outcome. This analysis was performed separately for each of the 47 hypotheses (7 at the group level and 40 at the individual level [i.e., 4 individual-level hypotheses x 10 subjects]). We also employed multiple logistic regression to account for multiple independent variables, each representing a distinct step in the analysis. This method allowed us to assess the simultaneous impact of these analysis steps on the probability of obtaining a signiﬁcant result in hypothesis testing. Prior to multiple logistic regression, we tested any multicollinearity between the processing pipeline steps that explain the variability in the hypothesis testing outcomes signiﬁcantly (i.e., Pruning, HRF Estimation Method, and Signal Space) via a chi-squared test. This test is often applied to explore the association between categorical independent variables by identifying signiﬁcant relationships between pairs of such variables. In this study, we conducted contingency table analysis to generate frequency distribution tables that illustrate the joint occurrences of categories for each pair of categorical independent variables. Subsequently, the chi-square test of independence was applied to evaluate the presence of signiﬁcant associationsbetweenthecategoricalvariables,whichyieldedbothateststatisticand a p-value. We established a p-value threshold of 0.05 for both the logistic regression analysis and the chi-square test. Visualization of processing steps. We used Sankey diagrams (Python) to visualize essential processing steps and parameters the participating groups employed for signal analysis and statistical testing (Figs. 2, 3). The reported choice of methods, parameters, or regressors are encoded as nodes in the diagram. Each node belongs to one of several categories (for instance, a category of methods, such as “Artifact Rejection”), which make up the diagram’sverticalstages.Thisvisualizationenablesbothaquantitativeanda qualitative assessment of the (co)occurrence and divergence of methodological choices across stages/categories in the analyses.
